sourceBindings.text: Rice, bread made from wheat, beans, tomatoes and apples all begin as crops. Sort them by use, then ask what plant part is harvested and what evidence a grower needs. This step teaches the groups. Later steps in this station will match crops with soil and climate, explain rotation, and build a plan; naming a group alone is not a site recommendation.

Why might maize grow well in one location but poorly a few kilometres away? Why might a grower vary a field's crop sequence? Think of soil condition, water, climate, nutrients, pests and management. A repeated crop is not automatically forbidden; its effects depend on the crop, field and controls. Write an initial explanation, discuss it with a partner, then revisit it after the lesson.

Start with the 5-minute food opener. Then think alone for 1 minute, discuss in pairs for 2 minutes and share for 2 minutes. Revisit both questions after learning; each learner records their own revision. A detailed rotation plan follows later.

sourceBindings.text: This lesson uses four practical groups: grains or cereals, legumes, vegetables and fruits. They are a useful classroom and farm-management lens, not a complete botanical taxonomy or a local regulatory crop list. A crop can have a botanical identity, a harvested organ and a culinary or market use at the same time. Use the stated lens before deciding where an example belongs.

Another classification can group carrots, potatoes and beets as root and tuber vegetables. That is a grouping by harvested parts and use, not a claim that all three are botanical roots. It illustrates a different classification lens; it is not an Egyptian regulatory list.

sourceBindings.text: Cereals are grasses grown chiefly for edible, often starch-rich seeds. Examples include maize (corn), rice, wheat, barley, sorghum and oats. Their grain supplies energy and is frequently produced at scale. Compare cereal crops using their actual nutrient demand, yield, fertiliser, roots and residue management rather than assuming one identical requirement.

Dense fibrous roots can contribute to soil structure. Cereal shoots and roots can return organic material if residues remain; harvest and residue removal can export nutrients and carbon. A high-yielding maize crop may need substantial nitrogen, but it is inaccurate to say every cereal always depletes organic matter. Balance depends on inputs, outputs, climate and management.

sourceBindings.text: Legumes produce pods. Examples include soybean, kidney and black beans, lentils, peas, peanut and alfalfa. Beans and lentils harvested for dry seed are pulses; peanut and soybean are oilseed legumes, and alfalfa is a forage legume. Green peas eaten fresh are vegetables in culinary use, although the plant is botanically a legume. Thus 'legume' and 'pulse' are not interchangeable names for every listed crop.

With compatible rhizobia and suitable conditions, nodules on legume roots can fix atmospheric nitrogen for plant use. The amount fixed, harvested, left in roots and residues, and available to the following crop varies. A legume cannot promise to replace all fertiliser or guarantee a positive nitrogen deposit. Confirm nodulation and assess the field and crop plan before estimating a credit.
Legumes are valued as protein-rich food crops; the crop’s use still distinguishes dry pulses, oilseed and forage legumes.

sourceBindings.text: Leafy examples are lettuce, spinach and cabbage. Carrot, radish and turnip are harvested for roots. Tomato, pepper and cucumber are fruiting vegetables by culinary use; their harvested organs are botanical fruits. Celery and asparagus are sometimes placed together in a 'stem vegetables' teaching row, but the crisp part usually eaten in celery is a leaf stalk (petiole), whereas asparagus is a young shoot or stem.

Potato and sweet potato can both be called tubers in everyday speech, but their harvested organs differ: potato is a stem tuber; sweet potato is a storage root. The distinction makes a plant diagram and its questions accurate. Root development may benefit from a sufficiently loose, unobstructed rooting zone; it does not prove a single compulsory soil texture. Leaf growth needs adequate nitrogen, but the amount depends on crop, measured soil supply and management. Carrot is an example that often prefers loose sandy loam; this is not a requirement for every cultivar or site. Drainage, compaction and cultivar still matter.
Vegetables contribute vitamins, minerals and fibre; crop cycles and nutrient needs vary widely.

sourceBindings.text: Examples include apple, orange, grape, strawberry, blueberry and banana. A fruit in botanical terms develops from a flower; the practical fruit-crop group is about production and use. Many orchard trees and vines stay in the ground for years, but these six examples do not all share the same plant form or management cycle. Strawberry and banana especially show why 'every fruit is a tree or bush' is false.

Long-lived plantings require sustained soil, drainage and root-zone care. Actual root depth and site suitability differ by crop, variety, rootstock and field. Do not infer that all fruits belong on clay or that any crop automatically suits an Egyptian field from its group label.
Many fruit crops are valued for sweetness, vitamins and antioxidants. Nutritional and management characteristics vary by crop.

sourceBindings.text: A simple analogy compares cereals withdrawing from a soil bank and legumes depositing into it. The picture is useful for remembering that harvest exports nutrients and some legumes can biologically fix nitrogen. It is not an accounting formula: both crops may remove nutrients at harvest, and the next crop's benefit depends on fixation, residue return, loss and measured soil supply.

In the four-panel illustration, cereal fibrous roots, legume nodules and carrot's enlarged edible taproot support discussion. Its paired sand/loam/clay crop labels and root-depth marks are schematic, not measured evidence or crop-specific soil rules. Treat the diagram as a comparison prompt, not a planting plan. A real crop choice also needs soil structure, drainage, pH, salinity, climate and water information.
